transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I can’t seem to turn the worrying off once it starts. I’ll tell myself I’ve made the list, checked the dates, done everything I reasonably can, but my mind just keeps going over it anyway.
Do you find yourself checking things over and over, even after you already know they’re okay?
I don’t think so, not really. I mean, I might look once more if I’m unsure, but I wouldn’t say I’m checking things over and over after I know they’re okay.
Are your worries mostly about many different parts of your life, or mainly about one specific problem?

It’s more many different parts of my life, I’d say. My mind jumps from the exhibition schedule, to my daughter’s travel plans, to whether the gutters on the house need fixing. And then small things start to feel like they could turn into something much bigger.
When the worrying starts, do you feel able to stop or control it?
Not really. Once it gets going, I can tell myself I’ve done what I can—made the list, checked the dates, all of that—but it still keeps running in my head. I have a hard time shutting it off.
Did this worrying start after a particular stressful event or major life change?

Yes, I think it did. It’s been about seven months now, and it seemed to start not long after my friend died. I was trying to keep our projects going after that, and the worrying just sort of took hold.
Does your worrying feel out of proportion to what’s actually going on?

Yes, I think it does. I mean, the things are real enough, but my mind takes them much further than they need to go. I’ll think about the exhibition schedule, or my daughter traveling, or even the gutters, and suddenly it feels like any one of them could turn into a much bigger problem.
Have you been feeling unusually tense or on edge in your body?

Yes. I feel sort of wound up even when I’m just sitting at home. I’ll be in my living room and notice I’m tapping my fingers during a phone call, or I’ll get up to straighten something because sitting still makes me feel jumpy.
Since your friend died, has the worrying stayed mostly centered on that loss and the responsibilities that came after it?

Not really just that, no. It started around then, but now my mind wanders all over. I’ll worry about the exhibition schedule, then my daughter’s travel plans, then whether the gutters need fixing, and each little thing starts to feel like it could turn into something much bigger.
Over the past six months, have you been worrying on most days?
Yes, most days. It’s been going on for about seven months now, since shortly after my friend died and I was trying to keep our projects moving.
Has this worrying been interfering with your day-to-day life?

Yes, somewhat. I still manage my usual things, like the garden and book club, but I’m not as on top of them. I’ll show up less prepared than I used to. And with the exhibition planning, I’ve started turning down pieces of it because it just feels harder to manage now.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really been keeping track of my sleep closely. Some nights feel more restless than others, but I don’t know that I’d say for sure it’s a major problem.
Have you been feeling easily tired?

Yes, I have. Even if I sleep through the night, I can wake up feeling like I’ve already done half a day’s work. And then after something small, like watering the garden beds or sorting papers for book club, I need to sit down and collect myself.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed a big problem with concentrating, at least not in any clear way. Sometimes I’m a little distracted, but I couldn’t say it’s something major.
Have you been feeling more irritable than usual?
I’m not sure I’d say more than usual. I get a little short now and then, but I haven’t really noticed a big change in my temper.
Have you been having muscle tension?

Yes, I do. By the evening especially, my shoulders and neck feel really tight, like I’ve been holding myself braced all day. I’ll notice I’m clenching my jaw too, even when I’m just reading or planning garden center activities.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?
Not really, no. I have off days like anyone, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been feeling depressed.
Do you feel your level of worry has been much greater than most people would have after your friend died?

Yes, I think so. Since then my worry seems to spread out over everything. My mind goes from the exhibition schedule to my daughter’s travel plans to whether the gutters need fixing, and then little things start feeling like they could turn into much bigger problems.
Would you say this worrying causes you a lot of distress?

Yes, it does. I’m still keeping up with the garden and book club, but I’m not as prepared as I used to be. And I’ve been turning down some of the exhibition planning because it just feels harder to manage now.
Has this worrying caused a big drop in how well you’re functioning day to day?

I wouldn’t say it’s been a big drop, no. I still keep up with the garden and book club. But I’m less prepared than I used to be, and I’ve started turning down parts of the exhibition planning because it just feels harder to manage.
Are the responsibilities that came after your friend’s death still going on?
Yes, they’re still there in a way. It’s been about seven months now, since shortly after my friend died and I tried to keep our projects moving.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes excessive anxiety and worry about multiple domains occurring on most days for about seven months, with difficulty controlling the worry, associated somatic symptoms (feeling keyed up, fatigue, muscle tension), and clinically significant distress with mild functional impairment. Anxiety is sufficiently specified, so unspecified anxiety disorder is less appropriate.
